CEST-detectable metabolite candidates: liver

2 of 3 candidates clear the simulated with-vs-without contrast threshold (0.5%) at some field strength, by chemical exchange (downfield, +ppm) or by the relayed NOE (upfield, −ppm). 1 fall below it; 0 are unknown because no group had a verified reference rate, so nothing could be simulated. The threshold applies to our own simulation, never to a literature MTRasym.

  • glycogen (glucosyl-unit equivalent pool): ✓ detectable (rNOE)
  • mobile protein/peptide amide pool (APT): ✓ detectable (chemical exchange)
  • glycosaminoglycans (GAG disaccharide-unit equivalent pool): ✗ not detectable

Excluded before simulation (not stored in the tissue): [model's own exclusion] Choline/choline-containing compounds (total Cho peak at 3.2 ppm): Composite MRS peak (glycerophosphocholine + phosphocholine + free choline) - per rules, spectroscopic category label, not a single chemically defined species. Free choline has no exchangeable protons (quaternary ammonium has no labile H; single -OH present but at <0.3 mM concentration). Excluded.; [model's own exclusion] Phosphocreatine/creatine: Normal liver has <1 mM total creatine because liver exports creatine; animal studies show ~0.3-0.5 mM in baseline (PMID 9515004, 11665842). Guanidino -NH2 has very slow exchange at pH 7.4 (pKa ~12.5). Excluded.; [model's own exclusion] Glucose (free): Liver free glucose is <1 mM due to rapid phosphorylation by glucokinase. Blood glucose (5 mM) is not parenchymal tissue concentration. Excluded.; [model's own exclusion] Glucose-6-phosphate: Liver G-6-P is ~0.1-0.3 mM (PMID 811498 mentions increase in fetal liver but still sub-mM). Below 1 mM threshold.; [model's own exclusion] UDP-glucose: ~0.3-0.5 mM (PMID 811498). Below threshold.; [model's own exclusion] Lactate: Fed liver lactate ~0.5-2 mM, borderline. Marginal but included for reference. Lactate has -OH (exchangeable) but the chemical exchange rate is very slow (alcohol).; [model's own exclusion] AMP, ADP: 0.1-0.5 mM each, below 1 mM threshold.; [model's own exclusion] Inorganic phosphate (Pi): ~1-2 mM in liver. Has fast-exchanging -OH (phosphate) giving CEST at ~5-6 ppm. Borderline candidate. Included for reference.; [model's own exclusion] Bile acids/bile salts: Primarily in bile canaliculi/secretion, not parenchymal cells at high concentration. Per rules, secretions excluded.; [model's own exclusion] Triglycerides/fatty acids: No exchangeable protons relevant for CEST.; [model's own exclusion] Urea: ~5-8 mM in liver. Has two -NH2 groups but exchange rate is extremely fast (>10,000 s⁻¹), not detectable by CEST at conventional RF powers.; [model's own exclusion] Creatine transporter substrates/endogenous ouabains: Either not endogenous (drug metabolites) or too low concentration.

glycogen (glucosyl-unit equivalent pool) — CEST: ✓ detectable (rNOE)

Concentration: 280.00 mM typical (100-450 mM glucosyl-unit equivalents depending on prandial state; fed ~300-450 mM, fasted ~80-200 mM)

Estimated concentration — no direct literature value found. Reasoning: PMID 22891360 reports 38.1 mmol/kg (38.1 mM) glucosyl units measured by 1H MRS at TE=35 ms, but this is a severe underestimate because glycogen's T2 (~15-25 ms) means >70% signal loss at this TE -- the authors acknowledge this limitation. Classic biochemical assays (Nilsson & Hultman, Scand J Clin Lab Invest, 1973) and 13C MRS studies (PMID 32157774) consistently report fed-state human liver glycogen as ~250-450 mM in glucosyl-unit equivalents. For CEST simulation, the relevant value is the concentration of glucosyl repeating units (not whole glycogen molecules), with 3 exchangeable hydroxyl protons per glucosyl unit. Fed-state: ~280 mM; fasted: ~100-180 mM. Per internal glucosyl unit: n_exchangeable=3 (-OH at C2, C3, C6). CEST peak ~0.5-1.5 ppm (glycoCEST). This is the most concentrated CEST pool in fed liver.

Recommended field strength(s): 0.5 T, 1.5 T, 3 T, 5 T, 7 T

Robustness to input uncertainty: robust

Uncertainty corners: Contrast over the uncertainty corners (aliphatic C-H (glycoNOE) [rnoe]: concentration 100-450 mM, kex fixed at 5 s−1 (single measurement, spread unknown)) at the swept B1/Tsat: 0.5 T: 0.38-1.68%, 1.5 T: 0.95-4.09%, 3 T: 1.59-6.73%, 5 T: 2.33-9.68%, 7 T: 2.62-10.82%. Threshold 0.5%. Detectable even at the low corner.

Frequency-collision analysis:

  • GlycoNOE (-1.1 ppm) at 0.5 T collides with GAG hydroxyls (0.82 ppm, 41 Hz separation < ~128 Hz linewidth) and semisolid MT (-2.4 ppm, 28 Hz < 16 kHz linewidth). At 1.5 T, GAG separation improves to 123 Hz but still marginally below linewidth (128 Hz).
  • At 3 T+, only the semisolid MT collision remains (166-387 Hz separation vs 16 kHz MT linewidth — always blurred). This is a universal MT overlap for upfield rNOE. The four hydroxyl groups are all degenerate at 1.0 ppm, merging into one pool. The amide APT pool at 3.5 ppm is well separated from glycoNOE at all fields.

Direct water saturation: At 0.5 T (B1=0.1 µT), direct-sat bandwidth 4.3 Hz; glycoNOE at -1.1 ppm is 57 Hz from water — no masking. At higher fields, bandwidth 10.6 Hz still small relative to offset. Hydroxyls at +1.0 ppm are closer to water but use same B1. No direct-sat masking of the dominant glycoNOE signal.

Ex vivo / in vivo exchange-rate caveat: Hydroxyl kex (31,850 s−1) is from an in vitro glycogen solution (PMID 38933551, mouse, phantom) measured via Swift-Connick transverse relaxation, not CEST, at unspecified pH. The glycoNOE effective rate (5 s−1) is a generic class-level rNOE value from protein-solution phantoms (PMID 25996515), not measured from glycogen. Both rates may differ substantially in vivo due to pH, temperature, and molecular crowding. This adds uncertainty to the simulated contrast values.

Optimized saturation sequence by field strength (derived from a Bloch-McConnell B1×Tsat sweep):

  • 0.5 T: B1=0.1 µT, Tsat=2000 ms, continuous wave (CW-equivalent B1,rms from simulation sweep) —
    recommended sequence: 1.056% contrast; no SAR ceiling applied
  • 1.5 T: B1=0.25 µT, Tsat=2000 ms, continuous wave (CW-equivalent B1,rms from simulation sweep) — Slow rNOE transfer (kex ~5 s−1) needs long Tsat at low B1 to build steady-state contrast. Higher B1 would increase direct water saturation and MT spillover with little benefit for this slow-exchanging pool.
    recommended sequence: 2.597% contrast; no SAR ceiling applied
  • 3 T: B1=0.25 µT, Tsat=3000 ms, continuous wave (CW-equivalent B1,rms from simulation sweep) — Same logic as 1.5 T; longer Tsat (3 s) increases SNR for the slow glycoNOE. 3 T glycoCEST experimentally demonstrated with Tsat ~2-3 s (PMID 26334509). Low B1 avoids direct-sat.
    recommended sequence: 4.310% contrast; no SAR ceiling applied
  • 5 T: B1=0.25 µT, Tsat=3000 ms, continuous wave (CW-equivalent B1,rms from simulation sweep) — Offset separation improves with field, but the optimal B1 (0.25 µT) remains low to avoid MT spillover from the broad semisolid pool. Contrast reaches 6.25%.
    recommended sequence: 6.252% contrast; no SAR ceiling applied
  • 7 T: B1=0.25 µT, Tsat=3000 ms, continuous wave (CW-equivalent B1,rms from simulation sweep) — Best contrast (7.0%) at 7 T. Low B1 (0.25 µT) keeps direct-sat minimal at this high field. The slow rNOE mechanism rewards long Tsat, not high power.
    recommended sequence: 7.016% contrast; no SAR ceiling applied

B1/Tsat vs. extraction method (click for note + literature)

Note: The glycoNOE (-1.1 ppm) is upfield, so MTRasym cannot isolate it cleanly (contaminated by downfield amide/NOE asymmetry). Use Lorentzian multi-pool fitting to separate glycoNOE from semisolid MT and other rNOE pools (PMID 39529314). At the optimized low B1 (0.25 µT), AREX (T1-normalized asymmetry removal) is also suitable to reduce direct-sat and T1 bias (PMID 25996515).

No citations.

Potential clinical impact

glycoCEST / glycogen NOE (0.5–1.5 ppm MTRasym): 3 CEST/NOE application and 3 metabolite-change studies verified (5 human, 1 animal; 46 humans, 0 animals; 3 dropped by verification). Glycogen (glycoCEST/NOE) imaged in human liver for feeding/fasting and in fatty liver; also in rat CCl4 model. Metabolite-change: lower glycogen in NAFLD steatosis and T2DM; massive accumulation in GSD-I/IV. Strong translational target for metabolic liver disease — no patient CEST study for NAFLD/NASH published yet.

Caveats / critique (9 points, 413 words) — Concentration 280 mM glucosyl units in hepatocyte cytoplasm is reasonable. Human liver glycogen ranges 100-450 mM glucosyl equivalents depending on fed/fasted s…
  • Concentration 280 mM glucosyl units in hepatocyte cytoplasm is reasonable. Human liver glycogen ranges 100-450 mM glucosyl equivalents depending on fed/fasted state, consistent with the range Agent 1 gave (100-450 mM). This is well within published estimates. No major issue. Group classes are correct: four hydroxyls (OH-2,3,4,6) classed as hydroxyl and aliphatic C-H classed as rnoe.
  • However, the chemist estimated kex ~10^5-10^6 s−1 for hydroxyls, but the reference-table value simulated was 31,850 s−1 — an order of magnitude slower. The chemist overestimated exchange rate. OH-6 shift estimated at 0.8 ppm versus simulated 1.0 ppm is a minor discrepancy. No exchangeable protons were neglected.
  • The simulated glycoNOE offset at -1.1 ppm is consistent with in vivo literature values: -1.0 ppm (PMID 39529314 mouse muscle) and -1.2 ppm (PMID 42076810 mouse muscle). The hydroxyl shift at 1.0 ppm matches the value used in human liver glycoCEST studies (PMID 36161668, 26334509). No large discrepancy between in vivo and simulated shifts. None.
  • The chemist correctly identified all four hydroxyls plus the aliphatic C-H (glycoNOE) per glucosyl unit. verifying_citations: PMID 26334509 (claimed as 'Chemical exchange saturation transfer (CEST) MR technique for in-vivo liver imaging at 3.0 tesla.') dropped
  • PubMed's actual title is 'Chemical exchange saturation transfer (CEST) MR technique for in-vivo liver imaging at 3.0 tesla.'. extraction_method_citations: PMID 39529314 (claimed as 'Multi-pool Lorentzian fitting of rNOE in mouse muscle') dropped
  • PubMed's actual title is 'Simultaneous monitoring of glycogen, creatine, and phosphocreatine in type II glycogen storage disease using saturation transfer MRI.'. extraction_method_citations: PMID 25996515 (claimed as 'AREX for exchange rate quantification') dropped PubMed's actual title is 'Transfer Rate Edited experiment for the selective detection of Chemical Exchange via Saturation Transfer (TRE-CEST).'.
  • no SAR or hardware ceiling is applied: the recommended B1/Tsat is the sweep optimum, and deliverability must be checked against the scanner's SAR monitor Structure NOT independently verified (no PubChem record found for this name or its aliases) -- shown as the chemist agent proposed it. Repeating glucosyl unit (-C6H10O5-). n_exchangeable=3 hydroxyls per unit.
  • Exchangeable-proton-equivalent pool = 280 mM × 3 = 840 mM hydroxyl protons. CEST peak at ~0.5-1.5 ppm (glycoCEST). Major established CEST target. Varies dramatically with prandial state (fed vs fasted).

mobile protein/peptide amide pool (APT) — CEST: ✓ detectable (chemical exchange)

Concentration: 85.00 mM typical (70-110 mM amide-proton equivalents (liver))

Estimated concentration — no direct literature value found. Reasoning: The CEST-relevant pool is defined by the equivalent concentration of exchangeable amide backbone protons from mobile proteins and peptides, expressed in mM of amide-proton equivalents (not the molarity of the protein molecules themselves). BSA phantom calibration from PMID 27272542 shows that 60 mg/ml BSA (a model mobile protein) yields ~80 mM amide-proton equivalents. Human liver has ~150-200 mg total protein/g wet weight, of which ~40-50% is mobile (cytosolic, non-membrane-bound), giving ~60-90 mg mobile protein/g. Applying the BSA calibration factor (80 mM amide/60 mg protein), liver mobile protein yields ~80-120 mM amide-proton equivalents. The APT signal in liver (PMID 26334509) is robust with MTRasym ~2.4%, consistent with this pool size. n_exchangeable=1 per peptide bond. Adopting 85 mM as a conservative working value.

Derivation stepValueSource
Total protein in human liver is ~150-200 mg/g wet weight150-200 mg/greference_work: Tietz Clinical Guide to Laboratory Tests, 4th ed.; also Geigy Scientific Tables Vol. 1 (liver composition)
~40-50% of total protein is mobile (cytosolic, not membrane-bound or structural)~40-50% fractionassumption: General biochemical knowledge: hepatocytes have extensive ER/membrane systems; cytosolic mobile fraction is ~40-50%
Therefore mobile protein = 150-200 × 0.4-0.5 = 60-100 mg mobile protein/g liver60-100 mg/gcalculation: Arithmetic from steps 1 and 2
BSA phantom calibration (PMID 27272542): 60 mg/ml BSA yields ~80 mM amide-proton equivalents~80 mM at 60 mg/mljournal_article: PMID 27272542; n=10 healthy volunteers, BSA phantom at various concentrations
Scaling: 60-100 mg mobile protein/g liver gives ~80-130 mM amide-proton equivalents. APT-CEST in liver (PMID 26334509) measured MTRasym ~2.4% (fed), confirming adequate pool size. Adopting 85 mM as conservative working value85 mMcalculation: Proportional scaling from BSA calibration to liver mobile protein content

Uncertainty corners: Contrast over the uncertainty corners (aliphatic C-H (rNOE) [rnoe]: concentration 70-110 mM, kex fixed at 5 s−1 (single measurement, spread unknown); backbone amide NH [amide]: concentration 70-110 mM, kex 15-158 s−1) at the swept B1/Tsat: 0.5 T: 0.41-0.64%, 1.5 T: 0.37-2.01%, 3 T: 0.47-3.82%, 5 T: 0.66-5.33%, 7 T: 0.74-5.92%. Threshold 0.5%. Detectable even at the low corner.

Frequency-collision analysis:

  • Critical collision: GAG amide (N-acetyl) at 3.5 ppm and APT amide at 3.5 ppm are degenerate (0 Hz separation). However, the GAG concentration (3 mM) is ~28-fold lower than APT (85 mM), so GAG contribution to the total amide signal is negligible (<0.1% vs ~1-3%). The collision is harmless — APT dominates.
  • Glycogen hydroxyls at 1.0 ppm are separated by 160-745 Hz (depending on field) from 3.5 ppm, which exceeds the amide exchange-broadened linewidth (~53 Hz) at all fields ≥1.5 T. The semisolid MT at -2.4 ppm is a broad background (16 kHz) but at 3.5 ppm the separation (753-1758 Hz) is resolvable with multi-pool fitting.

Direct water saturation: Direct-sat bandwidth 10.6-31.9 Hz across fields. At 0.5 T, amide at 3.5 ppm is 74 Hz from water; at 7 T, 3.5 ppm = 1040 Hz. The offset-to-bandwidth ratio exceeds 2:1 at all fields. No direct-sat masking of the amide signal.

Ex vivo / in vivo exchange-rate caveat: The amide kex (65.5 s−1) is a median of two brain in vivo measurements (PMID 40228056, 23008121), not from liver. Liver pH may differ from brain (~7.0-7.4 vs ~7.0-7.2); amide exchange is base-catalyzed. The rNOE effective rate (5 s−1) is from generic protein-solution phantoms (PMID 25996515). No liver-specific exchange-rate measurements exist in the reference table — both rates are borrowed.

Optimized saturation sequence by field strength (derived from a Bloch-McConnell B1×Tsat sweep):

  • 0.5 T: B1=0.25 µT, Tsat=2000 ms, continuous wave (CW-equivalent B1,rms from simulation sweep) —
    recommended sequence: 0.493% contrast; no SAR ceiling applied
  • 1.5 T: B1=0.5 µT, Tsat=3000 ms, continuous wave (CW-equivalent B1,rms from simulation sweep) — Slow-intermediate exchange (kex ~65 s−1). B1 of 0.5 µT is in the classic APT range; high enough to saturate the amide pool without excessive direct water saturation. Tsat of 3 s allows steady-state buildup.
    recommended sequence: 1.316% contrast; no SAR ceiling applied
  • 3 T: B1=0.75 µT, Tsat=3000 ms, continuous wave (CW-equivalent B1,rms from simulation sweep) — Higher B1 (0.75 µT) is feasible at 3 T because direct-sat bandwidth (31.9 Hz) is a smaller fraction of the amide offset (447 Hz = 3.5 ppm). Peak contrast 2.0%. Standard 3 T liver APT studies (PMID 26334509) use similar B1.
    recommended sequence: 1.984% contrast; no SAR ceiling applied
  • 5 T: B1=0.75 µT, Tsat=3000 ms, continuous wave (CW-equivalent B1,rms from simulation sweep) — B1 of 0.75 µT maintained; amide offset is 745 Hz (3.5 ppm at 5 T) — well separated. Contrast increases to 2.79%. Longer Tsat (3 s) continues to benefit the slow-exchanging amide.
    recommended sequence: 2.785% contrast; no SAR ceiling applied
  • 7 T: B1=0.75 µT, Tsat=3000 ms, continuous wave (CW-equivalent B1,rms from simulation sweep) — Best contrast (3.1%). Amide offset 1040 Hz from water. B1 0.75 µT corresponds to gammaB1/(2pi) ~32 Hz, well within slow-exchange regime (kex/delta_omega ~ 65/1040 = 0.06). 7 T offers best spectral separation.
    recommended sequence: 3.095% contrast; no SAR ceiling applied

B1/Tsat vs. extraction method (click for note + literature)

Note: Standard APT extraction uses MTRasym at 3.5 ppm, but this conflates upfield rNOE from -3.5 ppm with downfield amide CEST. At 3 T+, the rNOE contribution is significant. Use Lorentzian multi-pool fitting to separate amide CEST, rNOE, and MT (PMID 28272761, 26334509 used MTRasym in liver). AREX can remove T1 and direct-sat bias at low B1. For clinical translation at 3 T, simple MTRasym remains most common (PMID 32785767).

No citations.

Potential clinical impact

APT (amide proton transfer, MTRasym at 3.5 ppm): 2 CEST/NOE application and 0 metabolite-change studies verified (1 human, 1 animal; 56 humans, 0 animals; 5 dropped by verification). APTw CEST applied to liver: HCC grading (n=32, n=56) and TACE response prediction, plus rodent HCC models. Also brain APT in cirrhosis patients with HE. Metabolite-change: proteomics shows altered hepatic protein expression in cirrhosis, alcoholic hepatitis. Strong evidence for APT as HCC biomarker; no liver fibrosis/NASH APT study found yet.

Caveats / critique (9 points, 418 words) — Concentration of 85 mM amide units in hepatocytes is plausible. Typical hepatic protein content ~150-200 mg/g wet weight gives ~1.4-1.8 mmol/g amino acid residu…
  • Concentration of 85 mM amide units in hepatocytes is plausible. Typical hepatic protein content ~150-200 mg/g wet weight gives ~1.4-1.8 mmol/g amino acid residues; converting to tissue water yields ~80-120 mM. The range 70-110 mM is reasonable.
  • However, the APT pool in liver includes all mobile proteins — cytosolic, membrane-associated, and serum albumin in blood (~0.6 mM in plasma, ~10-15% liver blood volume). The estimate may be slightly low but is within acceptable bounds. Group class assignment is correct: backbone amide NH (3.5 ppm) classed as amide; aliphatic C-H (-3.5 ppm) classed as rnoe.
  • The chemist estimated kex 20-200 s−1, and the simulated value (65.5 s−1, median of 15 and 116 s−1) falls within this range. No exchangeable protons were neglected. The aliphatic rNOE correctly identifies ~6 C-H protons per residue.
  • The simulated amide shift of 3.5 ppm is fully consistent with in vivo human liver APT literature (PMIDs 26334509, 26391991, 36161668) where the standard APTw measurement uses MTRasym at 3.5 ppm. No discrepancy. None. The chemist identified backbone amide NH and aliphatic C-H (rNOE) per residue.
  • Additional side-chain groups (e.g. amine in lysine, guanidinium in arginine, hydroxyl in serine/threonine) are present on amino acid side chains but are not part of the APT-centered pool and were reasonably omitted. verifying_citations: PMID 26334509 (claimed as 'Chemical exchange saturation transfer (CEST) MR technique for in-vivo liver imaging at 3.0 tesla.') dropped
  • PubMed's actual title is 'Chemical exchange saturation transfer (CEST) MR technique for in-vivo liver imaging at 3.0 tesla.'. extraction_method_citations: PMID 28272761 (claimed as 'Lorentzian separation of APT and rNOE in brain') dropped
  • PubMed's actual title is 'Accuracy in the quantification of chemical exchange saturation transfer (CEST) and relayed nuclear Overhauser enhancement (rNOE) saturation transfer effects.'. extraction_method_citations: PMID 26334509 (claimed as 'MTRasym APT in liver at 3 T') dropped PubMed's actual title is 'Chemical exchange saturation transfer (CEST) MR technique for in-vivo liver imaging at 3.0 tesla.'.
  • no SAR or hardware ceiling is applied: the recommended B1/Tsat is the sweep optimum, and deliverability must be checked against the scanner's SAR monitor Defined by repeating peptide bond (-CO-NH-). Pool concentration expressed as mM of amide-proton equivalents. n_exchangeable=1 per backbone amide. CEST peak at ~3.5 ppm downfield from water (APT-weighted CEST).
  • Concentration changes with nutritional state (autophagy during fasting reduces mobile protein). This is the most established CEST metabolite target in MRI. glycosaminoglycans (GAG disaccharide-unit equivalent pool) — CEST: ✗ not detectable

Concentration: 3.00 mM typical (0.5-6 mM disaccharide-unit equivalents (normal liver); ~40-80 mM in cartilage for comparison) animal evidence only

Estimated concentration — no direct literature value found. Reasoning: The GAG pool is defined by the repeating disaccharide unit, not the whole proteoglycan molecule. Each disaccharide unit has ~3-5 exchangeable protons (sugar -OH, N-acetyl -NH, sulfate -OH). Cartilage has ~40-80 mM disaccharide units producing strong gagCEST. Liver GAG content is ~0.05-0.2% wet weight by biochemical assay, giving ~1-4 mM disaccharide units. However, in cartilage the gagCEST signal originates from the highly concentrated GAG network in the ECM. Liver lacks this dense GAG matrix. Therefore the effective exchangeable-proton pool is much lower in liver. The value 3 mM disaccharide-unit equivalents is the theoretical concentration from wet-weight assays; the true CEST-visible pool is likely <<1 mM. No published gagCEST study has demonstrated signal in normal liver parenchyma. Excluding for practical purposes.

Threshold 0.5%.

Frequency-collision analysis:

  • Severe: The N-acetyl amide at 3.5 ppm is perfectly degenerate (0 Hz separation) with the 28-fold more concentrated APT amide pool. The hydroxyl groups (0.82 ppm) collide with glycogen hydroxyls (1.0 ppm) at all fields (37-53 Hz separation at 5 T vs ~5 kHz exchange-broadened linewidth — fully merged).
  • The unsimulated N-sulfo NH at ~2.0 ppm, if present, would sit between the amide and hydroxyl pools and could be partially resolved at 7 T, but no data exists to simulate it. The rNOE pool was not simulated due to format limitations.

Direct water saturation: At 5 T, hydroxyl groups (0.82 ppm = 174 Hz from water) have direct-sat bandwidth 42.6 Hz — partial overlap at the highest B1 used (1.0 µT). At 0.5 T, hydroxyls at 0.82 ppm are only 17 Hz from water; they are largely masked by direct saturation. The amide group at 3.5 ppm is well separated at all fields.

Ex vivo / in vivo exchange-rate caveat: The amide kex (65.5 s−1) is borrowed from brain amide measurements. The hydroxyl kex (600 s−1) is borrowed from myo-inositol in human brain (PMID 20951217), not from GAGs. No GAG-specific exchange rate exists in the reference table. The N-sulfo NH amine group has no reference data at all — its exchange rate and shift are completely unknown for liver. All rates have high uncertainty.

Potential clinical impact

gagCEST (MTRasym around 1 ppm): 0 CEST/NOE application and 1 metabolite-change studies verified (1 human, 0 animal; 0 humans, 0 animals; 4 dropped by verification). No gagCEST liver imaging exists — all gagCEST studies are in cartilage (osteoarthritis).   • Concentration of 3 mM disaccharide units in liver ECM is very low. This is far below the ~50-100 mM GAG in knee cartilage where gagCEST has been demonstrated. At 3 mM, the simulated contrast reaches a maximum of 0.105% (at 7 T) — well below the 0.5% detectability threshold.
  • Agent 1 should have noted that liver GAG concentration is likely too low for CEST detection. The range given (0.5-6 mM) is reasonable for liver heparan sulfate but does not change the conclusion. Group class assignments are chemically correct: N-sulfo NH (amine), N-acetyl amide NH (amide), hydroxyls (uronate and glucosamine), and aliphatic C-H (rnoe).

The hydroxyl exchange rates (600 s−1) are borrowed from myo-inositol, not from GAGs. The simulated N-acetyl amide at 3.5 ppm matches the standard amide offset.

The N-sulfo NH amine group would be expected at ~2.0 ppm but was not simulated due to missing reference data. The chemist correctly identified all exchangeable groups per disaccharide unit. In vivo verification: ROI-differential CEST scan — Axial slab centred at T9 vertebral level through the porta hepatis

Why this scan:

  • An axial slab through the porta hepatis simultaneously images liver (high glycogen, moderate protein), spleen (low glycogen, high protein), renal cortex (near-zero glycogen, moderate protein), and paraspinal muscle (intermediate glycogen, high protein).
  • Glycogen's ~1 ppm OH signal should scale with tissue concentration (liver >> muscle >> spleen >> renal cortex), while APT's 3.5 ppm amide signal should track mobile protein content (spleen ≈ muscle ≈ liver > renal cortex). This ROI-contrast pattern discriminates true metabolite-specific CEST from generic MT/NOE, which appears similar across tissues at a given offset.
ROIWhere it is drawnRole
liver target tissueEntire visible liver parenchyma on slices 3-7, excluding vessels >5 mm, bile ducts, and gallbladder fossatarget tissue; high glycogen (~280 mM), moderate mobile protein (~85 mM amide equivalent)
spleenSplenic parenchyma on slices 3-6, avoiding hilar vesselscomparison tissue; low glycogen (~10 mM), high mobile protein (~100 mM amide equivalent)
renal_cortexOuter renal cortex of right kidney on slices 4-5, avoiding medullacomparison tissue; near-zero glycogen (~1 mM), moderate mobile protein (~70 mM amide equivalent)
paraspinal_muscleErector spinae / psoas major group, drawn on slices 3-7, avoiding vertebral bodycomparison tissue; intermediate glycogen (~80 mM), high mobile protein (~100 mM amide equivalent)

Scan protocol: 3 T, Gaussian pulse train, B1=0.5 µT, 120 pulses × 15 ms (interpulse delay 10 ms, duty cycle 60%), total Tsat=3000 ms, TR=4000 ms

SAR reasoning (the experimentalist agent's own; the pipeline applies no SAR model): At 3 T, body-coil transmission with 60% duty cycle, 0.50 μT mean B1, 3 s saturation per 4 s TR yields time-averaged B1² ≈ 0.075 μT². For a 70 kg adult with 10 axial slices, whole-body SAR is well below 2 W/kg (FDA limit). No local RF hotspots in liver.

Compromise rationale:

  • Glycogen OH (fast exchange, ~1 ppm) favours 0.25 μT to avoid excessive line broadening; APT amide (slow exchange, 3.5 ppm) favours 0.75 μT for efficient saturation. At 0.50 μT, glycogen's ~280 mM concentration still produces detectable signal with ~60% of its optimal saturation, while APT receives ~67% of its optimal B1 (0.75 μT).
  • The 3 s saturation time matches both agents' recommendations. This B1 undersaturates glycogen relative to its optimum and gives APT moderate saturation; neither pool is fully suppressed at this compromise.

Fat suppression: SPAIR (Spectral Attenuated Inversion Recovery) prepulse, TI ~180 ms at 3 T to null fat. Required because visceral and subcutaneous fat surround the liver, and hepatic steatosis is common; unsuppressed fat CH2 signal at ~1.3 ppm would confound glycogen OH signal at ~1.0 ppm. SPAIR preferred over SPIR for better B1-insensitivity at body-coil transmission.

Motion mitigation: Free-breathing with respiratory triggering (navigator on right hemi-diaphragm at end-expiration). Each offset acquired during ~3 s quiescent period. Total scan: 18 offsets × 3 s = 54 s per average; 2 averages = 108 s main Z-spectrum + ~30 s WASSR = ~2.5 min. Alternatively, multiple 4 s breath-holds at end-expiration per offset for cooperative patients.

Slice coverage: Axial slab, centre at T9 vertebra (porta hepatis level), 10 contiguous 5-mm slices (50 mm total coverage), FOV 350×350 mm. Slices 1-2 cover liver dome and lung interface; slices 3-7 cover main liver parenchyma, spleen, kidney, and paraspinal muscles; slices 8-10 cover liver tip and bowel interface.

Structures in FOV: liver, spleen, right kidney (renal cortex), paraspinal muscle (erector spinae, psoas), vertebral body (marrow) - not drawn, bowel (partial, lower slices), diaphragm/lung (upper slices)

Differential analysis plan:

  • 1. ROI-average Z-spectra after B0 correction (WASSR map), normalized to M0 at +8 ppm. 2. Compute MTRasym(Δω) = [Z(-Δω)-Z(+Δω)]/M0 per ROI. 3. Glycogen hypothesis test: MTRasym(1.0 ppm) rank order should be liver > muscle > spleen > renal_cortex by >2× SEM across voxels. APT hypothesis test: MTRasym(3.5 ppm) rank order should be spleen ≈ paraspinal_muscle ≈ liver > renal_cortex. 4.
  • Lorentzian difference fitting: subtract a 3-pool model (water, MT, rNOE) from each Z-spectrum; residual at +1.0 ppm and +3.5 ppm gives the metabolite-specific component. If the residual pattern matches the concentration gradient, the metabolite is confirmed; if all ROIs show the same residual (or rank order mismatches), the signal is likely non-specific MT/NOE baseline.

Not actively targeted: GAG disaccharide-unit equivalent pool: excluded because the physicist agent reported low simulated contrast at all field strengths for liver GAG. Liver has negligible GAG content (~0.1 mM, far below cartilage). Adding GAG offsets would increase scan time without discriminant power.

Caveats:

  • Partial-volume effects: 5 mm axial slices may mix liver with diaphragm/peritoneum at dome/tip, and renal cortex is thin (~5-8 mm). B0/B1 inhomogeneity: liver-lung and bowel-liver interfaces cause susceptibility gradients up to 0.5 ppm even after WASSR correction; body coil transmit B1 varies ±30% across FOV requiring B1 mapping.
  • Single-compromise B1 (0.50 μT) undersaturates glycogen's optimal regime (0.25 μT) and APT (0.75 μT), reducing contrast-to-noise. Liver motion from cardiac pulsation (left lobe) and respiratory drift may exceed trigger window. Signal from fat-water chemical shift at ~1.3 ppm may incompletely suppress in steatotic livers. The 8 mM amide concentration uncertainty across ROIs limits quantitative rigor.

  • sweep_b1_grid_uT: [0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 2.5, 3.0, 4.0, 5.0, 6.0]
  • sweep_tsat_grid_ms: [500, 750, 1000, 1500, 2000, 3000]
  • sweep_saturation_model: continuous wave, single shot from thermal equilibrium (CW-equivalent B1,rms)
  • b1_ceiling: no SAR or hardware ceiling is applied: the recommended B1/Tsat is the sweep optimum, and deliverability must be checked against the scanner's SAR monitor
  • tsat_choice: grid Tsat with the highest contrast at the best B1 (no scan-time shortening)
  • pool_t1_s: 1.0
  • pool_t2_s: 0.01
  • max_background_metabolites: 3
  • verification_scan_field_T: 3.0
  • verification_scan_model: the experimentalist's pulse train (rectangular pulses at its B1), 90 degree single-shot readout, exact periodic steady state at its TR, Z normalized to the same cycle without saturation
  • b1_inhomogeneity_fraction: 0.3
  • uncertainty_corners: contrast re-simulated at the swept B1/Tsat at every corner of [concentration range from the literature agent] x [kex spread of the reference tier]
  • llm_sampling: each model's served defaults; the pipeline sends no temperature or top_p

A FAILED completeness check means the agent's structured output never covered everything it was asked to (e.g. a verdict for every metabolite) within its retry budget, and the incomplete output was kept; the deterministic checks above flag what is missing.
